opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think it's a really interesting example, because on the surface it doesn't look like reinforcement learning at all. There's no gradient update, no policy network being trained with PPO or anything like that. The weights of the language model are frozen. But if you step back and look at the structure of what's happening, it has all the ingredients of an RL loop.

You have an agent acting in an environment, Minecraft, and it gets feedback from that environment. It writes code, executes it, observes what happened, whether it succeeded, what errors came back, what the state of the inventory is, and then it uses that feedback to improve its behavior. That's trial and error learning, which is really the essence of reinforcement learning.

What's different is where the learning happens. Instead of updating parameters, Voyager accumulates knowledge in a skill library, essentially a growing collection of programs it has verified to work. So the "policy," if you like, is the combination of the frozen language model plus this ever-expanding library of skills and the context it's conditioned on. Learning happens in that external memory, in the prompt, rather than in the weights.

And then there's the automatic curriculum, which I find particularly exciting. The language model proposes the next task for itself based on what it has already achieved, things that are just at the frontier of its capabilities, not too easy, not too hard. That connects very directly to work on open-endedness and unsupervised environment design, where you want an agent to keep generating its own challenges so it keeps learning.

So I'd say it's reinforcement learning in the broader sense: an agent improving its behavior through interaction and feedback from an environment. It's just that the language model gives you very strong priors, human knowledge about what's interesting and how the world works, so you can explore much more efficiently than an agent starting from scratch. And I think that's one of the most promising directions right now: using foundation models as the engine for open-ended exploration, while still grounding them in environment feedback.

r001.rationale: It notes that Voyager has no gradient updates and frozen model weights, explaining why it may not look like reinforcement learning on the surface, before distinguishing the broader sense.

r002.rationale: It describes learning through a growing external library of verified, reusable programs.

r003.rationale: It says the agent uses environmental feedback—such as outcomes, errors, and inventory state—to improve its behavior through trial and error.

r004.rationale: It contrasts frozen weights with broader reinforcement learning, but does not say that LLM systems work well empirically while fitting awkwardly into established theoretical categories.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, that's a great question, because at first glance it doesn't look like reinforcement learning in the classical sense at all. There's no policy network being trained with gradients, there's no value function, no reward signal in the way we'd normally think about it. The weights of the language model are frozen. So if you define RL narrowly as "we have a parameterized policy and we update its parameters using a reward signal," then Voyager isn't doing that.

But I think that's too narrow a view. If you go back to what reinforcement learning actually is as a problem formulation, it's an agent interacting with an environment, taking actions, observing consequences, and improving its behavior over time based on those consequences. And Voyager is doing exactly that. It has an automatic curriculum that proposes tasks, it attempts them in the environment, it gets feedback from the environment, including error messages and whether the task succeeded, and then it iteratively refines its behavior. It's doing trial and error in the environment, which is the heart of RL.

What's interesting is where the learning happens. Instead of learning being stored in the weights, it's stored in a skill library, in these pieces of code that it has written and verified, and in the context that gets fed back into the model. So you could say the "policy" is the language model plus the skill library plus the prompting scaffold, and that composite system is what's improving. The update rule just isn't gradient descent anymore, it's something like in-context learning combined with this external memory of skills.

And honestly, I think this is one of the more exciting shifts in the field. We spent years in deep RL learning policies from scratch, with enormous sample complexity, because the agent had to discover everything about the world from a reward signal alone. Now we have these foundation models that come in with huge amounts of prior knowledge about how the world works, how Minecraft works even, and the question becomes: how do you combine that prior knowledge with the kind of interactive, exploratory learning that RL is about? Voyager is one answer to that, where the exploration and the credit assignment are happening in natural language and code rather than in parameter space.

So I'd say it's RL in spirit, in terms of the problem it's solving, even if it's not RL in terms of the algorithm you'd find in a textbook. And I suspect that distinction will matter less and less, because the really interesting systems going forward are going to combine both, using these interaction loops to generate experience and then also updating the models on that experience.

r001.rationale: It says Voyager’s language model weights are frozen and that it does not update policy parameters using reward, so it is not classical RL under that definition.

r002.rationale: It describes learning as stored in a skill library of programs Voyager writes and verifies, which are reused through external memory.

r003.rationale: It characterizes Voyager as RL in a broader sense because it interacts with the environment, observes consequences and feedback, and refines its behavior.

r004.rationale: The response says Voyager fits RL in spirit but not the textbook algorithmic sense. It does not clearly claim that LLM-based systems work well empirically.

astra-6.text:
I think it depends on how broadly you define reinforcement learning. In the broad sense, you have an agent interacting with an environment, observing what happens, and using that feedback to improve its behavior. Voyager fits that picture: the language model generates code to do something in Minecraft, gets feedback from executing it, and can revise that code. It also accumulates a library of skills that it can reuse.

But that’s different from reinforcement learning in the more conventional sense, where you’re updating the parameters of a policy to maximize expected return. The language model itself isn’t being trained through those interactions. The adaptation is happening through its context and through the skills being stored outside the model.

So I’d describe it as an agent that learns through interaction, with a very powerful pretrained model doing much of the work. Whether you call that reinforcement learning is partly a terminology question. The interesting question for me is what it can discover through that interaction, and how far it can go beyond the capabilities already present in the pretrained model.

r001.rationale: It says the model itself is not trained through the interactions and contrasts this with conventional RL, where policy parameters are updated to maximize expected return.

r002.rationale: It says Voyager accumulates a library of skills for reuse and that the skills are stored outside the model.

r003.rationale: It describes an agent observing environmental feedback and revising its behavior through interaction.

r004.rationale: It calls the terminology partly a question of definition, but does not state that LLM-based systems can work well empirically while fitting awkwardly into existing theoretical categories.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it depends on how broadly you define reinforcement learning. Voyager has this loop where it interacts with an environment, observes what happens, and uses that feedback to improve what it does next. In that broad sense, there’s certainly a reinforcement learning flavor to it.

But it’s not reinforcement learning in the conventional sense of updating a policy’s parameters to maximize expected return. The language model generates code, gets feedback from executing that code, and revises it. Successful behaviors can then be stored in a skill library and reused. So the improvement is happening through prompting, program generation, and an external memory, rather than through updates to the language model’s weights.

I’d describe it as an agent that learns through interaction, while being careful to distinguish that from the specific optimization algorithms we typically mean by reinforcement learning.

r001.rationale: It says Voyager does not update the language model’s weights, contrasting that with conventional reinforcement learning’s policy parameter updates.

r002.rationale: It explains that successful behaviors are stored in a skill library and reused.

r003.rationale: It describes Voyager as learning through interaction, using environmental feedback to improve what it does next.

r004.rationale: It distinguishes Voyager from conventional reinforcement learning, but does not say LLM systems can work well empirically while fitting awkwardly into established theoretical categories.
